To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the divergence of a focused diffraction-limiting pump beam can be reduced by a factor of five by using the Raman scattering process in a liquid medium.
the divergence of a stimulated Raman scattered beam is reduced to 1/5th of that of the incident pump beam.
a five-fold reduction in beam divergence of the Stokes beam was observed as a result of wavefront reversal under stimulated Raman conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a new class of optical devices, based on the nonlinear interaction of light with matter, which will be useful for applications in laser fusion and other fields of science and technology.

the development of new methods for the generation of coherent Stokes radiation in a variety of media and with the application of this radiation to a variety of problems in nonlinear optics, laser spectroscopy and laser technology.
the generation of a high power Stokes beam by stimulated Raman scattering of a focused pump beam.

, in a diffraction-limited geometry, a focused pump beam of wavelength 1.064μm and diameter 0.2mm, focused to a spot of diameter 0.1mm, can be used to produce an output Stokes beam with a divergence of 1.3×10−3 rad, a beam diameter at 1/e2 of the intensity of 0.5mm, and a peak power of 0.3MW.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the divergence reduction is a general feature of stimulated Raman backscattering in focused beams.
the divergence reduction is due to the fact that a wavefront reversal of the Stokes beam is achieved in this process.
the divergence of the Stokes beam was always less than the divergence of the pump beam, and that the Stokes beam could be made to have the opposite direction of propagation to the pump beam.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the wavefront of a Stokes beam can be reversed in a diffraction-limited focused laser pump beam under stimulated Raman conditions.
the divergence of the Stokes beam can be reduced significantly, even in the presence of diffraction-limited focusing, by using the appropriate experimental geometry.

, by exploiting the nonlinear optical properties of the medium and the wavefront reversal phenomenon, we can achieve a significant reduction in the divergence and a corresponding increase in the energy of the Stokes beam, which may be useful in applications such as laser-driven fusion.
